MR. RAPP  ADVICE TO MEMBERS BY LAW BRANCH OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I am rising on a question of privilege affecting all hon. members of this house. Yesterday Your Honour ruled out of order two private members' bills, giving as a reason that they were money bills. One hon. member appealed your ruling and a division followed in which your ruling was upheld.
Your Honour will recall that on a previous occasion you ruled one of my own bills out of order for a similar reason, as being a money bill. At that time I accepted your decision-reluctantly, nevertheless gracefully. That is one reason I voted yesterday to uphold your ruling. The other is that I felt politically bound-and this would not concern Your Honour-not to support the appeal.
My point of privilege is that it came to the attention of hon. members that the assistance which private members receive from some officials of the law branch who help draft these bills seems to be at variance with the opinion of other law branch officials who communicate with Your Honour on these matters. This is a point which affects all hon. members and unless these difficulties are resolved to the satisfaction of all, private members' bills will eventually disappear from the order paper, which in the opinion of many hon. members would be a tragedy, to say the least.

maintopic: MR. KNOWLES  OPINION OF DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL ON VALIDITY OF CERTAIN APPOINTMENTS

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MR. KNOWLES  OPINION OF DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL ON VALIDITY OF CERTAIN APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday the Prime Minister tabled a document which is identified as sessional paper No. 39B. It contains an opinion given by the deputy attorney general on the validity of certain arrangements made for appointing special advisers to the Minister of Finance.
My point of privilege can be very succinctly stated. In addition to the affront which I believe was already given to parliament by the manner in which these men were
appointed, the matter is now compounded by our being asked to accept as approval of these appointments a document which in itself admits there were no provisions for the arrangements which were made, but that it can be "construed" that there was proper authority.
This opinion of Mr. Driedger, which was presented to the house by the Prime Minister, who therefore has to take responsibility for it, says quite clearly that there are two subsections of the government contracts regulations under which these appointments might have been made, but that they cannot be made under either of those subsections. One of these subsections sets out the classes of contracts which can be made-transportation, snow removal, garbage removal, and that kind of thing-and Mr. Driedger says that the contracts in question do not come within any of those categories. The other subsection has to do with contracts which do not exceed a certain amount of money. Mr. Driedger says there is no guarantee that they will not exceed that amount, and therefore they do not come under that subsection.
Having removed these arrangements from any provision set out in the government contracts regulations, he says:
Although the government contracts regulations do not express in positive terms that a contract for services under which more than $1,000 is payable may be entered into with the approval of treasury board, they have been construed as authorizing a contracting authority to enter into such a contract with the approval of the treasury board-
My point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that what we now have is precisely what we had last June. We have the government construing that the Financial Administration Act or regulations made under it gives them authority to do something which the act itself says cannot be done. The Financial Administration Act says that no appointments by the treasury board can be made under it. The government contracts regulations themselves say that no appointments can be made under them. But the government, by construing that it has such authority, is doing something which I submit is contrary to the provisions of the act and the regulations made thereunder. Last year hon. members who are now in office strongly objected to the action of the then government in construing that it had the right under the Financial Administration Act to bring in the surcharge order. Now

Tabling Report on Supply the same hon. members are doing the same thing, construing that they have a right which the deputy attorney general says is not specifically set out.
I think this matter calls for very serious consideration by parliament, because the relations between the executive and parliament depend upon the government paying attention to the letter of statutes, and not governing by construing.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraith (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while it is not my intention to make a lengthy statement on the first item, I think I should take a few minutes of the committee's time to deal with some matters. I believe those hon. members attending their first session would particularly appreciate a brief explanation of the extent of government activity in transportation, a field which I think all hon. members would agree is of decided importance to the economy of our country. It is quite possible that in doing so I may fail to mention certain items which hon. members will consider of major import. In many instances this may be because I have dealt already with the particular matter when answering a question during the session or in discussions with hon. members from the areas concerned.
The main estimates tabled by the Minister of Finance on May 29 contain a total of $231,038,000 to be voted for the needs of the Department of Transport. In addition there are certain statutory items and various sums to be voted for the several related agencies. These latter figures are readily available in a general summary set out in the blue book.
I think I should go through the main estimates first and content myself with remarks about them. The activities in our marine services are such that the standard of service rendered for shipping generally is being improved substantially and continuously year
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
after year. Our shipping construction program is similar in size to that of last year. Strong support was received for the decision to provide eight high speed cutters to improve the marine search and rescue operations. By the end of July 1963 four will be in service, and all will be in operation by this fall. The department in this year's estimates is provided with $1,282,800 toward this construction.
Another large item relates to the new weatherships which will replace the existing obsolete ships in the manning of Pacific weather station "PAPA". Tenders have been called for the first vessel and construction will commence very soon. It is anticipated that three progress payments totalling $2,700,000 will be made by March 31, 1964. The department will be ready to contract for the second vessel by the fall of 1963 and the amount of $450,000 has been allowed in the estimates for the payment due on the signing of the contract.
Last year special mention was made of an unusual type of ship, namely an icebreaking cable repair vessel. The current estimates contain $4,021,000 for this ship, which is under construction at Canadian Vickers Limited, Montreal. A depot ship for the accommodation of stevedores for the off-loading of military and civil cargo at far northern sites was accepted last month. The Canadian coastguard ship Vercheres, built in 1901, has been replaced with a new vessel, the Canadian coastguard ship Montmagny completed last month. Contracts have been placed with Allied Builders Limited, Vancouver, for the construction of a tender for Prince Rupert and a work boat for the Mackenzie river.
Still on the subject of vessel construction, I might mention that $300,000 will be expended on the preparation of plans and specifications for northern supply ships, a small icebreaker for the lakehead, a vessel to replace the Saurel and Chesterfield, and an icebreaker for the Charlottetown agency. The design of the triple screw icebreaker, construction of which was approved in 1959, is practically complete and a contract will be let during the fiscal year, $750,000 having been provided to cover the payment due on signing the contract.
On the operational side the appropriation for the operation and maintenance of the coastguard fleet is up by over $1 million to a total of $21,680,000, and here again northern work is a big factor. A substantial amount of this is reimbursed to the government for northern supply work done for others. The program initiated some years back to modernize the marine agency depots is coming along quite well, and we contemplate a further outlay of some $2.4 million this year.

Expenditures for administration, capital construction and equipment for the marine works program, which covers marine aids to navigation such as light stations, fog signals, buoys, lightships and the supporting marine agencies, will involve an outlay of some $11,940,000. The total number of marine aids maintained by the department under this program is about 15,000.
For administration and further development of secondary canals the estimates provide $4,351,000. Included in this is some $400,000 for a start on the new lock on the Trent canal at Swift Rapids and the initial planning for the new lock required at Big Chute. Two hundred thousand dollars each is provided in connection with the new lock under construction at Fenelon Falls and for the restoration of a dam at Campbellford, and $175,000 is included for the rehabilitation of the Peterborough lift lock.
During the past year the departmental officials have devoted considerable thought and effort toward reducing the hazard involved in the operation of small pleasure craft, which I am sorry to say seems to be increasing because of the increase each year in the numbers of these small craft on our inland waters. Last year the department introduced a scheme requiring pleasure craft in certain categories to fit plates bearing recommended load and horsepower limitations. While the limitations set out on the plates are recommendations only, and that is necessary because of the various conditions under which boats operate, it is felt that such guidance does restrain many inexperienced operators from excessive loading and powering, and this is particularly true when they are buying boats and engines separately. It is in this field where, regrettably, there have been many tragic drownings on our waterways.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Could I ask the minister a question? Does he have any figures as to the numbers of licences now issued for this type of boat?

When we come to the detailed items I will give what information I can. There is other supplementary information on the subject which can appropriately be given at that time. The issuing of these plates is a large effort in view of the tremendous number of small boats involved, and I must say that the boating public generally and the industry concerned are giving every reasonable cooperation to the department.
Small boat safety and small boat regulations are, as I have indicated, an increasing problem, particularly with regard to demands for licensing of boat operators and more
Supply-Transport
extensive licensing of boats. I have had in mind and have given some thought, attention and study to possible courses of action to deal with this situation which will require both further legislation on the part of the federal government and an approach involving the co-operation of the provinces in administration. I can perhaps deal with that aspect of the matter more appropriately when the expected legislation is before the house.
With regard to coasting vessels, in order that coasting vessels in Newfoundland may be drydocked for steamship inspection purposes the department is providing a slipway at Clarenville. It is hoped that this haul-out facility will go into operation in the spring of 1964. Its construction is the first phase of a project to provide a marine haul-out, transfer system and fitting out wharf at Clarenville, the total cost of which is estimated to be $549,000.
I should also like to speak briefly on the air services appropriations which cover the broad fields of civil aviation, telecommunications and meteorology, both in regard to capital programs and operating and maintenance programs. In total these votes represent approximately $135 million in the 1963-64 fiscal year.
The largest single appropriation once again is that contained in vote 155 entitled "Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment" with respect to national airports. While the vote is slightly over $38 million, this figure represents a decrease from the level of recent years. The terminal building program for international airports undertaken to meet the heavy traffic demands generated by growing acceptance of air travel is nearing completion and this, together with the fact that the large runway pavement construction program associated with the introduction of turboprop and jet aircraft at major airports has passed its peak, has tended to effect the reduction of this vote.
While new international terminals such as the imposing buildings under construction at Toronto, Winnipeg and Edmonton will be coming into operation this year, several trunk and feeder terminals at locations such as Fredericton, London, Sault Ste. Marie, the lakehead and Whitehorse are still in various stages of planning and construction and have been provided for in the vote.
Since the acquisition of the city of Vancouver's interest in the Vancouver international airport, planning for the international terminal has been advancing and action has already been taken on preparation of plans as well as on preliminary site development. Because of both the requirement for preloading the area due to the nature of the

Supply-Transport
area and subsequent time for settlement and the complexities of planning an up to date international terminal, it will probably be next year before tenders are called on the terminal building itself.
The current year's estimates represent the beginning of a trend in air services toward gradually decreasing capital expenditures on airport facilities. Offsetting this, of course, is the gradual increase in operation costs which it is expected will continue as public demands for expanding services continue to be satisfied in the aviation field. However, this needs to be measured against the airport revenue situation. Over the past three years airport revenues have increased from $9.1 million in the fiscal year 1959-60 to $15.6 million for the fiscal year 1962-63. While this increase has not been at a uniform rate, we expect this general trend to continue in future years.
Now, while I have indicated that capital expenditures for airport facilities will decline over the next several years, such a trend does not hold in the field of radio aids to air and marine navigation. Here, due to the continuing increase in the number, size and speed of aircraft, provision is being made for improvement in the efficiency and safety standards of the services. Procedures and equipment for handling traffic are continuing to become more complex, and while the level of the 1963-64 expenditures might indicate a stable condition, it is anticipated that significant increases may have to occur in the years immediately ahead if our facilities are to be adequate for the growing traffic.
There is also provision in vote 180 for the department to enter the field of international space communication. This activity will be in the area of operational experimentation and testing, by provision of a ground station to participate in international communication by satellites. The objectives are to assist our common communications carrier industry engaged in international communication and the development of the use of this new media, and at the same time to assist in focusing the attention of our communications manufacturing industry on this new field.
In the field of meteorology, construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, vote 200, the main projects are the continuation of the program to instal transmissometers and ceilometers at our international airports to provide information on landing conditions during marginal weather. Also contained in this vote are funds for the procurement and installation of weather radar at Halifax, Toronto, Winnipeg and Edmonton. In the field of upper air soundings, funds have been included to initiate a program to

equip the upper air stations with new equipment capable of measuring meteorological conditions up to 100,000 feet.
In addition to the estimates of my department I am submitting those of related agencies or bodies including, the national harbours board, a statutory crown corporation which administers the principle deep sea Canadian harbours. The main and supplementary estimates of the board for 1963-64 amount to some $18 million, and the money will go toward the construction or reconstruction of transit sheds, wharves, grain elevator systems and other works at certain ports.
As the national harbours handle the bulk of Canada's overseas trade, which I think again all hon. members will agree is of vital concern to the national economy, the development and maintenance of these ports has kept and must keep pace with traffic and shipping demands. As Canadian ports compete for foreign cargoes with ports in the United States, it is especially important that facilities and services provided at Canadian ports be kept adequate, efficient and economical to use. In its efforts to remain competitive the national harbours board works closely with other Canadian transportation interests such as the railways, trucking companies and shipping lines. Close liaison is also maintained with exporters, importers and domestic shippers, and the board consults and co-operates with the Department of Trade and Commerce in the promotion of direct trade between Canada and foreign countries.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises me that the task of preparing the 1964 report to government on the sufficiency of tolls to meet its statutory obligations is proceeding as planned in full co-operation with the United States seaway development corporation. In so far as operations for the 1963 navigation season are concerned, the authority reports that for the months of April, May and June tonnage has increased by 1,250,000 tons over the same period of 1962. In the same three month period revenues have increased over those of 1962 by some $625,000 I may say at the moment there is considerable study, at a very active stage I might add, being given to the question of twinning the locks of the Welland canal.
The Canadian maritime commission is responsible for the capital subsidies for the construction of commercial and fishing vessels. During 1962-63 funds totalling $22.5 million were paid out in respect of construction of 110 ships. Of these 94 were completions and 16 were in various stages of completion. The aggregate value of ship construction involved

in the subsidies was approximately $79,835,000. For the fiscal year 1963-64 capital subsidies lor this purpose in both the main and supplementary estimates will total $30 million.
I have not had the responsibility of office long enough to complete a full review of major aspects of transportation policy, but I have been sufficiently long in office to ascertain the major matters which in my opinion need prompt attention, and to initiate studies of these. Paramount, of course, and I think all hon. members will agree, is the matter of legislation affecting the railways of Canada in order to eliminate the present massive temporary subsidies and to provide a new framework for future rationalization to meet the increasing competition of other modes of transport. I have been engaged in discussions with a great many interested groups, including representatives from some of the provinces very directly concerned, on the whole subject of proposed legislation arising out of the MacPherson royal commission report on transportation. Much work on this subject had been done by my immediate predecessor in office, the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I have been carrying that on from the point where I believe he left off.
I am quite sure he will understand when I say that, while I have been carrying on from the point where he left off, my continuation of this study and some of the things I found in the course of this study so far will undoubtedly lead to some adjustment in the proposals that were to be brought before parliament. I would not want him to believe that the continuation of the studies, which has been taking a great deal of my time, would merely result in the presentation of the legislation that he had been preparing. There are some major points on which further study has revealed the need for a somewhat different approach, and I hope he will appreciate that.
I expect to have this proposed legislation ready for submission to the house later in the session. I hope the program of the house will be such that at that time it can be dealt with, because I believe it to be of major importance to the economy of this country. I believe that to be a view which is shared by a great many hon. members on both sides of the house.
I have also come to the conclusion that a careful review of major aviation policy as it affects our scheduled air services, and carriers providing these services, is necessary. I believe that some clarification of the relationships and future role is essential to meet the rapidly changing technical and economic circumstances of aviation, and the highly competitive world of international aviation. What this may involve I am not prepared to
Supply-Transport
say in any firm way until the review has been fully completed, but some fairly substantial changes may be needed to protect our national and international position and prevent us from weakening and dissipating our efforts.
As for the field of shipping and shipbuilding, I believe the program initiated by my predecessor has produced useful results, particularly for the shipbuilding industry and other related sectors. I will keep this program under continuing review. Apart from this I have little to add at present, other than to note that various representations, suggesting the need for something more in the way of a shipping policy, all seem to involve additional government subsidies. I can say quite frankly this is not an easy or attractive prospect, and I am reminded that the MacPherson royal commission on transportation stressed in general the need to allow each mode of transport to compete with other modes without subsidizing one at the expense of another.
I have also commenced, with my departmental officials, a review of the general machinery of transportation under the Minister of Transport. I subscribe to the view expressed, I believe, by the MacPherson royal commission and touched on by the Glassco royal commission that this country can best be served by an over-all, integrated approach to transportation. At this stage I am inclined to feel that improved arrangements for coordination of policy, as among the various agencies outside the department which report to me, may be desirable, but I have not yet decided how best this can be achieved. This is another subject that is getting quite active attention at the moment, and I hope to make some changes in this regard in the relatively near future. When I say that I mean within a very few months. It is one of the matters I consider of utmost importance.
Mr. Chairman, I hope this brief and general review will simplify and expedite consideration of the estimates which I respectfully submit to the committee for its consideration and approval.
Before concluding my remarks I must repeat something I said on one occasion on orders of the day. While I do not find orders of the day disagreeable, there are times when I find one has to over-abbreviate replies, and one is not able to explain the subject in quite the way one would wish. However, when I was asked my very first question as minister I took the opportunity to express to the former minister of transport my thanks for the courtesy he showed me on the day I was sworn in as minister. It is perhaps a very small thing, but under our processes of

Supply-Transport
government it is one which I regard as very important, and I want to have it on record when transport matters are being considered here. I therefore repeat my acknowledgment of that courtesy.

Mr. Chairman, my first words are of congratulation to the minister on presenting the estimates of the Department of Transport for the first time, and on his appointment as head of that extremely interesting department. I thank him personally for the kind words he expressed about me, and I can assure him that I am quite convinced, when the government changes again, I shall receive the same treatment from him. Anyway I thank him very much for the sincerity of his expressions.
Transportation is definitely a major industry in a country of the size and importance of Canada, even more so than in any other country in the world. Transportation as an industry in itself is of tremendous importance for the services it is called upon to render to the population of Canada, and it is even more important for the tremendous role it plays in the development of trade and industry in a country which lives on external trade. In fact transportation is one of the key factors in the position of Canada as a major exporter.
The government headed by the present right hon. Leader of the Opposition was very conscious of this importance of transportation, and I am sure any independent observer would agree that during the last five years great things were accomplished by the Department of Transport and by the previous government in matters of transportation. When saying that I want to pay tribute to the staff of the department for their wonderful devotion during my term as head of the department. The Department of Transport is a huge department and a modem one. Many things happen in transport, and there is a lot of work for any minister; but during the period I was in charge I always had the good fortune of being able to rely on devoted public servants.
I do not want to make a complete review of everything accomplished by the previous government in transportation matters during the last five years, but I do wish to deal with some of the major problems our administration was faced with and the solutions that we brought forward for the benefit of the Canadian people. During those years Canada took great strides forward in shipping, aviation and railways. Today our position is sound because the previous government dealt with many major problems. However, in transportation things change so rapidly that new problems are created every day. We

might not have settled all the problems, but we certainly attacked them with vigour and determination.
I should like to deal with these three fields separately, and first I shall discuss shipping. At the end of the second world war we had 10,000 Canadians employed on deep sea ships and about 18,000 others on coastal vessels and lakers. During the term of office of the government of our predecessors, Canada's deep sea fleet was allowed to disappear completely, and the same fate was facing our lake and coastal fleets on the St. Lawrence with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. Our lakes fleet was protected by the barrier of small canals between the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river, but unfortunately it was composed of old ships which were at a disadvantage, compared with foreign ships, immediately the seaway was opened. In addition, replacements were very difficult to secure owing to the fact that the wages we pay in Canadian shipyards do not compare with wages paid in Europe or Japan. As far as our fishing fleet was concerned, it was also in a most inferior position vis-a-vis European fishermen, starting with Russia. We have probably the best fishermen in the world, but they were handicapped by the fact that they were manning ships which were too old or too small and which could not go far enough out to sea in order to catch the fish. Our fishermen were in the sad position of having to observe huge fleets of modern vessels coming from across the Atlantic to fish right off our shores.
The previous government decided to attack this problem, and in attacking it we took into account the position of our shipyards. We all know the tremendous effort the shipyards of Canada were called upon to make during the war. They expanded at that time, but unfortunately around 1957 the shipyards were facing tremendous problems. All that was left to them were direct government contracts. That was the situation in 1957 when our government took office. We decided to take action. We set up a subsidy policy that has given Canada good, fast, modern ships. This policy also brought about full activity in our large shipyards. At the present time our fleet of lakers is a first class one and I think we can face the competition of foreign vessels in this area.
As far as fishing trawlers are concerned, the new subsidy has meant a great deal to maritimers and the fishermen of our east coast. At the present time all our small shipyards are busy building fishing trawlers. The federal government pays a subsidy of 50 per cent in connection with this shipbuilding. We have given the tools to our Canadian fishermen to go out and compete

with the fishing fleets of the world. Indications are that our fishermen are really increasing their fleet and the program is working extremely well, thanks also to the co-operation of provincial governments in many cases.
Another problem facing our shipping was that of the coastal shipping treaty we had with other members of the commonwealth. Of course the government hesitated before making a decision in this regard. We carried on an investigation of the situation and discovered that this commonwealth treaty did not mean anything today compared with what it meant in 1930 or 1932. One could see some strange situations. You had a group of United States financiers forming a small company in Nassau, with only a telephone and a girl to operate the telephone. A ship was registered in Nassau, the ship was built in Japan, owned in United States, manned by Italian officers and a Chinese crew, and plying Canadian inland waters because it was a commonwealth ship.
This situation was becoming absolutely impossible, and for that reason we decided to take action. We first extended the inland waters of Canada to include such harbours as Seven Islands and Havre St. Pierre, where our great steel mining industry carries on its activities. We notified Great Britain of our intention to withdraw from the treaty and asked her to contact the other commonwealth signatories to the treaty and obtain their agreement to this action. This enabled us to withdraw from the treaty and restrict our inland waters from Havre St. Pierre to the end of the lakes to Canadian flag ships. I think this measure will help our coastal fleet and will assist shipping carried out on the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes. Our action in this regard has produced a great deal of activity in the Canadian shipping world.
Of course it does not settle the matter of the deep sea fleet, but I can assure the house that before the election we were working on some very interesting plans to try to deal with this problem. Canada has a very good seagoing tradition. During the war we had a very large deep sea fleet. I think it is very important for a country which is an exporter, such as Canada, to have a certain number of deep sea ships. Let us not forget that the transportation of our goods to the countries to which we export is a very important factor, and we have a foreign exchange deficit of between $100 million and $150 million in transportation itself. Let us not forget also that the millions of bushels of wheat exported from western Canada to China were all carried in foreign ships. Therefore I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Transport will
Supply-Transport
study this matter and find a solution. We have assured the necessary protection to our coastal, lakes and fishing fleets. I think the next step is to deal with the problem of the deep sea fleet.
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to turn to another field of interest in transportation. I refer to the field of aviation. Aviation in a country such as Canada is a natural. During the five years we were in power we pushed with determination our airport building projects, not only to keep up with the present needs but also to plan for 10 or 12 years in advance. As a result we have in the main cities of Canada large, functional and modern terminals which compare advantageously with those of any country in the world. One has only to see Montreal airport on a Friday night, for instance, to realize that this magnificent air terminal was needed. Another interesting point is that the Montreal airport, even though it is a huge and very modern building which cost a great deal of money, is a paying proposition for Canada. I am sure that as aviation develops all these investments would prove to have been good investments. We have pushed very hard for Toronto to make progress in regard to Malton international airport. I had hoped that this matter might be terminated by last June, but my information is that it will be some time in the fall. It is going to be an important addition to the Toronto area and will provide much needed accommodation for the public.
After the war our regional carriers were in a very sound position due partly to the very advantageous D.E.W. line contracts. These contracts represented many millions of dollars. They were awarded every year, and practically all our regional carriers made progress as a result of these contracts. However, the contracts came to an end and the position of the regional carriers became extremely difficult. We asked the air transport board to make a complete review of all the permits, routes and schedules of the regional carriers. This important inquiry was held across Canada with sittings in all the major cities which had a special interest in aviation. After this review the pattern was revised and special areas were allocated to each of our regional carriers. This new scheme has been in operation for a few months now, and the picture is very encouraging. The new scheme gives efficient service to the population and I think that must always be the key purpose of these enterprises.
We had a difficulty in connection with the milk run. As Your Honour knows, Trans-Canada Air Lines wanted to withdraw from the operation of this run. It was, of course, a deficit operation, but it was one of extreme

Supply-Transport
importance to the population of western Canada. We were faced with the problem. T.C.A. wanted to get out of this route because they had to use DC-3's and they had only two of them; it was an expensive proposition for them to maintain anything but turboprops or pure jets in their fleet. We arranged for the transfer of this route to Transair, and I am informed that the service now is very good and that the population is satisfied with the service it gets in this area.
As hon. members know, we have two major air lines in Canada, one government owned and the other a private corporation. Our government tried, I think with success, to achieve a proper balance between the two. It was not always easy. Both air lines have very aggressive management which is essential in a field such as international aviation. During those five years we witnessed the advent of the large pure jet carriers of the DC-8 type. These huge carriers with their extraordinary capacity, tremendous speed and range, and especially their amazing technical perfection, really revolutionized aviation. But due to the high cost of these planes both air lines faced a period of heavy deficits. Fortunately these deficits are of a temporary nature and already they have nearly disappeared. They will be wiped out completely next year.
I should like to refer to one problem, in particular, which we had to face, the question of the development of the T.C.A. overhaul base in Winnipeg. As hon. members may recall, Trans-Canada Air Lines had decided that after the last Viscount had been overhauled in Winnipeg facilities there would have to close and the overhaul of both turboprop and pure jet planes would be carried out in Montreal. This decision had, of course, to be taken by T.C.A. at the time the $30 million base in Montreal was approved by the previous government. According to the president of T.C.A., this is when the decision was taken. However, thanks to the intervention of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and other hon. members from Manitoba the government to which I had the honour to belong made a very full inquiry at cabinet level at meetings with representatives of the provincial government, various interested municipalities, chambers of commerce and so on. We got from T.C.A. an undertaking to submit the whole matter anew to a firm of industrial consultants specializing in aviation so that a fresh study of the whole situation could be made. That was the position when we left office. I understand the new government is awaiting this report from the firm of consultants.

There is a further point I wish to raise. As you know, Mr. Chairman, Trans-Canada Air Lines has unfortunately never bought a plane built in Canada since the North Star. Now T.C.A. has to buy about 50 short to medium range pure jets. The previous government got from T.C.A. a commitment to obtain the approval of the government before it placed at least the final order for these planes. The purpose was to ensure that a complete investigation of all the possibilities of building the major percentage of the components of such planes in Canadian aircraft factories should be undertaken.
The results were most encouraging. All three possible suppliers of these aircraft have been negotiating with our aircraft industry and proposals, I am told, vary between 60 per cent and 100 per cent Canadian content. I think this is a most interesting and encouraging development, and one from which the Canadian people and in particular the Canadian aircraft industry will derive considerable benefit.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Can he provide some documentation or directives to this company setting out that policy? I have been unable to find any on that subject, though I have looked carefully.

I know there was a cabinet conclusion to that effect. I recall that I myself transmitted the decision of the cabinet to the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is, I am sure, recorded in the cabinet minutes. In addition it was, I am sure, agreed in writing by the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines that he intended to do this. I think it is an important and encouraging development when we consider that this involves contracts in the range of $250 million.
I should like to deal briefly now with the subject of railways. As the minister has said, one of the most important steps we took as an administration was the establishment of the MacPherson commission. When we took office Canadian National Railways were faced with huge deficits. Such deficits are most depressing for both management and employees. During our term of office we witnessed some very thorny labour relations problems in both Canadian railways. The men understandably wanted to get pay adjustments which they considered essential in view of the cost of living and the wages paid to employees in similar industries. Management was faced with the alternatives of a still larger deficit or higher freight rates. The government felt there were clear limits to freight rate increases on account of their effect on Canadian

producers and manufacturers. Our competitive position in the world markets could be jeopardized by any major freight rates increase. These freight rates are of the utmost importance, especially in the western provinces and in the maritimes.
Conscious of this deep-rooted problem, the government instituted the MacPherson commission with very precise terms of reference. This commission did a tremendous amount of work and produced a most thorough report containing a new philosophy and a wide, sweeping approach to the railway problem in Canada. As soon as it was in possession of this report the previous government set to work on the necessary legislation. Needless to say I agree with the minister that the preparation of this legislation was a tremendous job, and just prior to the last election our legislation was practically ready. I should have liked to see our government bring this legislation before the house because of the very hard work that has been done by some of my colleagues. I am sure the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings would agree with that. Much work was done by our cabinet committee on this matter and, of course by responsible officials. It was a very complicated piece of legislation embracing a vast field, with a tremendous impact on railway transportation in Canada.
I am very pleased to hear from the minister that this legislation is coming soon, and will probably be considered this year. I think it is a much needed step and is especially important when you think of the tremendous impact that the well-being of our railways has on the rest of Canada.
I think that is all I want to say at this moment, Mr. Chairman, but I should like the committee to realize what was accomplished by the previous government in the matter of transportation. I think we can say that we were faced with real problems and that we worked toward the solution of those problems. When we left office transportation in Canada had taken some major steps forward which I think was good for Canada as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, I see it is close to one o'clock, but there are one or two remarks I would like to make and some answers I should like to have from the minister regarding our consideration of the estimates today. I should like to know if at the same time we are studying amounts provided for the reduction in freight charges by the C.N.R. or the other railway company. Last year we used to pass those items in the standing committee before bringing them
Supply-Transport
to this committee. If we had passed these estimates before-I see the minister is ready to answer.

I think I could usefully answer that question now, Mr. Chairman. C.N.R. matters as such are not embodied in these estimates; they come under another item on the order paper, I think No. 7. That measure concerns the C.N.R. financing act and the financing of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The C.N.R. is not included in these estimates with which we are dealing today, but railways are the subject of one of the supplementary items. There is a major item involving the railways generally. Item 18 on the order paper is the motion to set up the committee to examine into the accounts, estimates and bills relating to the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines and with certain other powers. The practice has been for that committee to examine in a detailed way the annual report of Trans-Canada Air Lines and the annual report of the C.N.R. and all matters relating to the operations of those companies. Therefore I think it would be out of order to discuss the C.N.R. or T.C.A. today on these estimates.
If I may say so, the portion of the former minister's remarks concerning the purchase of T.C.A. aircraft concerns a matter which does not come under these estimates at all and should be discussed under the other two items on the order paper. It is a difficult line to draw. By the way, I hope that committee can be set up soon. I am ready and anxious to get it set up at the earliest moment, and I had put forward a proposal that the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines be reduced in number and that it do the work normally given to the special committee. I had undertaken to refer the two annual reports immediately that was done.
Can I ask a supplementary question. In view of the minister's explanation-
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor.

I assumed that the minister was speaking to a point of order, not answering a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No point of order was raised. I believe the hon. member who had the floor asked for some information.

Then let me raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Our party certainly

Supply-Transport
does not accept what seems to be a tendency on the part of the minister to suggest that the C.N.R. and all its ramifications, and that T.C.A. and all its ramifications, should not be discussed, and that they are not properly under these estimates. If that is a ruling, Mr. Chairman, we do not accept it. As a matter of fact we have five or six speakers who will be spending most of their time on Canadian National Railways matters.

I should also like to speak to the point of order. We should be able to discuss in a general way-and I think the minister may have gone this far-railway abandonment as it effects the C.N.R. and C.P.R. We should be able to discuss in a general way T.C.A. I do not think those items should be excluded, because railways in western Canada and other parts of Canada and the activities of T.C.A. are the most important features of the department. I think this question should be clarified before discussion proceeds.

I think it should also be clarified that if we are voting estimates for the C.N.R. and T.C.A. we should withdraw those estimates and first set up the special committee dealing with railways, canals and air lines and then come back to the estimates of the C.N.R. I should like some clarification of this point also. When I asked whether we were discussing the estimates of the railways I included vote 213a in the supplementary estimates, which concerns a payment of $20 million to provide payments to companies subject to order No. 96300 dated November 17, 1958, and also the $50 million payment resulting from the recommendations of the MacPherson commission.

I think this point of order should be resolved. Item 213a is a general item for railways and embraces the item in the former Freight Rates Reduction Act and the subsidies paid through the board of transport commissioners. It just happens that the C.N.R. is one of the railways concerned, so that in that indirect way there is something that goes to the C.N.R., but only in that indirect way. The financing and deficits of the C.N.R., as well as of T.C.A., are embraced in the C.N.R. financing act. The practice has been for that legislation to be referred to the special committee set up for the purpose of examining the accounts, operations and so on of the C.N.R. and T.C.A. That has always been the practice. In these estimates there is no direct vote either for T.C.A. or the C.N.R.
To come to the point raised by the hon. member for Bow River, it is quite true that you cannot discuss transport policy without

referring to the nationally owned railway system or nationally owned air line, but it is only in that context. Operational matters and other matters relating to their detailed financing and so on would properly be discussed on either of the other two items, the motion to set up the committee or the financing act itself. That is my point. I hope I have made it clear, and I would hope we could proceed in that way.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, it is not too clear. With regard to the items I have mentioned, the $20 million and $50 million payments by the board of transport commissioners, I think it has been the custom of the house to study them in the standing committee and not the other committee before studying them in the house.
That was never the practice.

That is what was done last year. We had the opportunity to study those two items in the standing committee, not a special or sessional committee but the standing committee. I cannot see why we should not do the same thing this year and study them in the standing committee. Therefore these two items should be withdrawn from committee of supply until the standing committee has had an opportunity to study them. I think the minister should give us this opportunity.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, since we have received the assurance of the Minister of Transport that he will stand item No. 213a in the supplementary estimates, I think this will permit us to study this item in the standing committee before we resume a detailed study of the estimates in the committee of the whole. I believe this procedure will permit us to go a little faster in our study of all the estimates of this department.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, there are several points to consider in the field of transportation. It might be noted, first of all, that the Department of Transport itself is probably one of the largest in the present government.
It must also be admitted that transportation is probably one of the most important means of communication between the Canadian people from all parts of the country. Thanks to our modern means of transportation, it is

much easier than formerly for people from one part of the country to get better acquainted with Canadians from another area.
In a country as large as Canada, transportation must be developed in order to foster a better understanding between the various areas and racial groups, especially the two main groups that make up our country.
Mr. Chairman, when we consider the estimates of the Department of Transport, we note that a great number of fields of endeavour are affected by transport, and therefore, by the Department of Transport: aviation, navigation, canal and railway services, grade crossings, etc.
The first point that comes to my mind is the following: All those areas must undergo some changes and must be brought up to date to meet modern needs, that is, they must develop and expand.
That is why, at the outset, I shall direct a number of questions to the minister. He might deal with them when he closes the discussion and provide answers if he deems it advisable.
Will the new 11 per cent tax levied on materials affect the Department of Transport in its development, its progress and its capital expenditure program with regard to railways, ships, wharves and canals?
If so, I submit that the minister should bring pressure to bear on his colleague so that the implementation of his department's main projects will not be affected by this tax on building materials. Otherwise, the progress of one of the most important departments would be slowed down.
Progress must not be hampered in the transportation industry because it is one of the industries that provide the most jobs in Canada and, therefore, is one of the prime factors of national growth.
Take, for instance, private industry. Considerable progress has been made there with regard to automobile plants, in assembly lines, various service stations, even gas stations, and motels. Add to that what has been accomplished by the provincial governments, such as bridges, roads, etc., and you will realize that the federal government must also do its share in this great industry, particularly with regard to railways, air lines, canals and navigation. The federal government must be in a position to develop those various services I have just mentioned and their progress must not be hampered by needless taxation.
Supply-Transport
In fact, in view of the degree to which private enterprise has developed and modernized, we realize that the transport problem is most alarming because the C.N.R., which is a crown corporation, is competing in such an irregular fashion with private enterprise that its competition practically becomes illegal.
Canadian private enterprise has succeeded in building up a trucking industry which provides a number of our fellow citizens with both employment and income. What happens? The government, through one of its crown corporations, the C.N.R., starts competing with the trucking industry which was set up by private enterprise.
It is noteworthy that the trucking industry shows a profit and pays taxes to the federal treasury, while the C.N.R., a crown corporation, not only does not pay taxes, but also show deficits which we, the Canadian citizens, must make up through our taxes. That is an abnormal situation.
Why should the government compete with private enterprise which has surpluses and pays taxes to the government, when the C.N.R. have deficits without paying any taxes? Such a situation is abnormal, and when one considers the figures one realizes that we give them rather substantial amounts. For instance, we see that the C.N.R. deficit for 1961 was $67,308,000, and $48,919,000 for 1962. And that does not take into account the many subsidies they received from the government. Apart from the $61 million deficit of the C.N.R. for last year, they received $80 million in subsidies of all kinds. We find that this C.N.R. item alone costs $150 million in taxes collected from the Canadian people, to make up for their deficit or fill the gap between their revenues and operation costs.
Mr. Chairman, if the government would instead see that the C.N.R. leave a business that does not concern them, leaving private enterprise to develop by itself the trucking industry which shows surpluses, the Minister of Finance would not have to tell the house this year: like our predecessors, we shall continue to grant subsidies to make up for some deficits. In our opinion, that should not be done, but we shall keep doing it anyway, because we have to do it.
The government should leave private enterprise in peace since it is efficient in that field whereas the government has met with failure. Mr. Chairman, we shall stress that particular point.

I shall not insist anymore today, since the minister agreed in a private conversation I had with him to stand item. No. 213a.
However, there is a matter on which we would endeavour to obtain as much information as possible during the discussion on the estimates for next year. We shall try to find through those items before us today what has been the part played by the French Canadians in the administration of public affairs and more particularly within the Department of Transport.
I have here some figures concerning the C.N.R. which I should like to quote and which give a quite accurate idea of what is happening in the Canadian National. In reviewing the various items we shall raise questions about the role played by French Canadians in the administration and in the awarding of D.O.T. contracts.
Why all those questions? Because we would like this government to recognize that the French Canadians should have a bigger place in the administration of the business of this country, so that they may realize that they are equal partners in their own country.

(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that these figures speak for themselves and can lead us to draw a conclusion.
The fact is that if French Canadians were allowed to take a more active interest in what is going on everywhere in the country, that is at the federal level, they would then be less inclined to withdraw into their shells as so many now do in the province of Quebec. I think that they should be allowed greater access to federal employment.
Last year, Mr. Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways-and this is only one example to illustrate the general idea that I want to set forth in the house-stated that French Canadians made up 11 per cent of all Canadian National employees, even though French Canadians amount to more than 30 per cent of the total Canadian population.
Incidentally, I have to congratulate Mr. Gordon for having appointed a French speaking vice-president. That appointment pleased

all French Canadians, and more particularly those in the province of Quebec, and we hope that the Minister of Transport will suggest to him that we want a few more, until we have our fair share.
However, I And that he added a few members to the board of directors. In contrast with previous years, Mr. Gordon did not even mention the board of directors, because that would be somewhat embarrassing for him. He also added section directors and assistant directors in Montreal and in the St. Lawrence district. I have to commend him for his know-how and ability in making us accept such conditions.
Those, Mr. Chairman, were a few preliminary remarks I wanted to make to illustrate my point. As a matter of fact, we think that, if the federal government granted our request in the field of transportation as we are discussing the subject today we would be most happy, and not because we want to boss everything, for that is not the case, but inasmuch as we represent nearly 30 per cent of the whole population, we believe we are entitled to our fair share and that this position should be considered.
Moreover, when we are studying the estimates, one by one, we shall try to find out the percentage of French Canadians working in each branch, as well as the salary scales, because that is precisely the responsibility of the investigation commission on bilingualism, if we want to establish the degree to which French Canadians are interested in taking part in this country's business, as they should, not only in the field of employment, but also with regard to building contracts, maintenance, repairs and purchasing.
That is the direction we shall give our questions during the discussion on the estimates.
In short, we are of the opinion that the Department of Transport is one of the most important departments which, through its various bodies, permits the establishment of relations between different areas and between the two great races and cultures making up this country.
It also enables the citizens of our country to become better acquainted. But we would like, when travelling in our country and using federal means of transportation to feel at home. And to illustrate my point, let me give you an example. When we are on a train between Montreal and Ottawa and there are two or three trainmen, it would be normal to have at least one of them who can speak French.

Also, when a plane leaves Montreal for Vancouver, with five air hostesses, it seems only just that one of them at least should speak French. Actually, things should be worked out in such a way that people from the province of Quebec and, for that matter, all Canadians would feel at home not only in their own province-be it Quebec, Ontario or Manitoba-but everywhere, from coast to coast.
The transportation facilities of the department can contribute materially to that end, that is to make French Canadians feel at home in the whole length and breadth of Canada.
English-speaking Canadians may rest assured that we shall do everything possible to greet them with all due warmth. They may find fault with certain situations, but we shall certainly do our best to correct those situations, for we want them to feel at home when they come and visit us. We shall address them in their mother tongue, and try and understand them, for we are convinced that a better understanding brings about a deeper appreciation.
