Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any department that more closely affects the people of Canada than the Department of Transport. I would like to join in the congratulations that have gone to the minister in taking over the portfolio. I would also like to say to the previous minister, the hon. member for Three Rivers, and his predecessor Hon. George Hees, that I feel they gave members of parliament excellent cooperation and, in a sense, opened up the department to inquiries and interests of members of parliament as well as they could.
The administration of the Department of Transport has never been, I think, severely criticized in this house since I have been here. This is, I would think, an accolade for the gentlemen who are the senior civil servants in the department. Yet I must confess that I felt somewhat disappointed when I heard that the hon. member for Ottawa West had been made Minister of Transport. I have always found him to be one of the most careful, meticulous members in this house and I have a tremendous respect for his integrity and sense of responsibility; but I did feel that the Department of Transport, because of the great needs to develop and fashion a new national transportation policy and a new national policy as outlined by the MacPherson report, might have drawn the

Supply-Transport
appointment by the Prime Minister of some member who had a great interest in transportation, or else was someone who was extremely interested in policy matters.
I hope the minister will forgive me if I say that I feel the very excellent qualities he has are complemented very much by his deputy minister, Mr. Baldwin. I think this may augur very well for the future administrative balance of the department. But I have always felt that the department, in its senior officials, has been somewhat tardy or hesitant; certainly I do not think they have been vigorously forthcoming in setting out new transportation policies, particularly as they cover the broad spectrum of transportation, rather than in specifics, I would be quite willing to concede that in the field of civil aviation the leadership from the senior civil service has been good. However, I do not think the Department of Transport in the last five or six years, in the whole question of railway operations and railway policy, the relationship of the truckers to such agencies as the board of transport commissioners, the relationship of air lines to the air transport board, the relationship of many harbours communities to the national harbours board, has been either especially energetic or leading to any goals that we can easily recognize and easily support.
The primary matter that has always intrigued the Canadian House of Commons, I suppose, since the creation of the railway boom away back at the time of confederation and before, has been the development of railway transport and its effects upon communities. Canadian National Railways year in, year out has borne the largest number of questions and greater interest than any other governmental agency of any kind. You can prove this in a random way just by skirting through the indexes of Hansard. At the present time Canadian National Railways and the railways as a whole are dead centre in the interests of very many hon. members of this house.
Just the other day the minister made an answer to representations that were put to him by a delegation from western Canada with regard to the announced plans of Canadian National Railways to go ahead with run-throughs in the middle of August. The minister's reply was to the effect that it was a matter for negotiation or relationship of a contractual kind between management and labour. I want to say to the minister that his answer is a typical one, typical over the past number of years, and it reflects an inability to recognize, on the part of the government, any kind of responsibility in this very touchy area. The minister will remember that the group which came to him and the

delegations from Rainy River, Melville and these other places did not ask him to interfere in labour-management relations. They asked him if he would use the position he holds to request the Canadian National Railways to postpone the introduction of these run-throughs until there was an opportunity to make a really good presentation of the whole matter. I should like to point out that the problem involved in these run-throughs has been developing all the way along in the relationship between the railways and their employees, as technological change has been advancing. We have never been able to get the government to accept responsibility for some of the dislocation caused or to place the responsibility upon the railways.
At the present time, through the action of this house, the subject matter of a bill I brought forward this session has been referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. The question I wish to put to the minister is this: Will he endeavour through the position he holds to see that these run-throughs are not proceeded with until that committee has had a chance to hear representations concerning changes in the Railway Act which bear directly on this problem? I say they bear directly upon it because these changes would spell out the responsibility of the railway both to the employees and to the communities which this kind of dislocation affects.
There are other hon. members who will, no doubt, wish to speak on this subject. I know that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will want to talk about it. I merely want to say that the relationship at the present time between the employees of the railways, particularly in western Canada, and their senior union leadership is very poor. This applies to both major railway companies but particularly to the C.N.R. I am not putting this forward as a fact that can be proven: It is my opinion. I feel this relationship has been worsened by various incidents which have taken place recently and I will mention one of these incidents as an example: The brotherhood of locomotive engineers had a strike vote of over 90 per cent, yet the leadership turned around and settled with the railways without obtaining a single gain beyond those they already had. It is because of suspicions like this existing between the majority of the membership and the unions that one finds such a group as the joint running trades committee, an unofficial group within the locals from Port Arthur to Vancouver, responding spontaneously to the challenge posed by these run-throughs.
I would like to tell the minister this: When I asked the Minister of Labour to get an

assessment made of the situation, I wanted him to make that assessment in order to make sure that the government realizes the threat which is implicit by mid August if the run-throughs proceed. If the railroaders have the same attitude then as they have today, I think there is going to be trouble. I think the minister should be prepared to accept some responsibility for this situation, even though he has denied in a statement he made in the house that this is a matter with which he can interfere. At least, that is my interpretation of what he said.
There is another subject on which I wish to comment in connection with the C.N.R. I want to touch on this matter of railway line abandonment. One of the striking things about the political pressures which have been developing in western Canada as a result of the line abandonment policies foreshadowed in the MacPherson report, is the fact that both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. have been, generally, lumped together. We do not find the distinction which is often made in this house between the government-owned railway and the privately-owned railway. I should like to tell the minister that this lumping together of the railways in so far as their actions affect public policy is something I should like to see extended into a number of other fields. It seems to me that, given the scope of the subsidies and support which the C.P.R. has been receiving in recent years from the national war chest, it is time we had the opportunity to meet the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway under some kind of formal arrangement in a committee of this house. I make this point because one cannot divide policy in Canada between a government-owned railway on one hand and a privately-owned railway on the other. If the C.P.R. were completely free of regulations or if it were not availing itself of the subsidies permitted to it-and I am not blaming the company for availing itself of these subsidies -I can see why we might leave this company to one side. But in present circumstances I think it is about time an opportunity of hearing the views of the president of the C.P.R. expressed before a parliamentary committee.
One of the questions I should like to ask the minister is this: Will he tell us where are the proposals put forward by Mr. Gordon? Mr. Gordon told us two years ago that he was presenting proposals to the minister of finance and the minister of transport with respect to the long term debt structure of the C.N.R. Since he became president in 1950 Mr. Gordon has changed his mind a number of times as to the factors which are preventing the C.N.R. from presenting a budget ending up in the black instead of in the red.
Supply-Transport
His latest representations seem to me to be to the effect that without a recasting of the debt structure of the C.N.R. the operation is never likely to end on the profit side of the ledger. I had a transportation economist look at the debt structure of the C.N.R. for me and he made the point that one of the reasons these debts are so immense is the large sums which have to be devoted to the repayment of interest charges.
In the last annual report of the C.N.R. for 1962, one finds that the total long term debt outstanding is $1,842,345,846. This is an enormous sum. My friend analysed the two ways in which the C.N.R. has been financing its operations in recent years, particularly with respect to its capital needs, taking care of some of its other long term debt as it has matured. There have been two ways of doing this. One was by the issue of debentures, and in recent years these issues have borne a high rate of interest-over 5 per cent at times. At other times the company has secured loans from government at very low rates of interest. My friend made an analysis as a result of which he told me that if the loans made over the past seven years had been made at a standard or low interest rate of 21 per cent of the total interest charge per year would have been some $350 million less than it is. That is a huge sum to be saved by the C.N.R. had this debt been built up on the basis of an interest rate of 2| per cent. My hon. friend in the Social Credit party could probably make a more effective analysis of that kind of interest rate, but it seems to me ridiculous that the long term debt of the Canadian National Railways, which is a government corporation, should be bearing interest charges as high as 5J per cent, as is the situation at the present time.
I have been very critical, as have other hon. members of our party, of the way Mr. Gordon has operated the Canadian National Railways. He has certainly spent money with abandon I think there have been tremendous results in improving the operations of the C.N.R., but the point is that the debt structure which it bears at the moment is immense. Proposals have been presented to the government over the last two years to alter and to change it, and I think it is time members of this house were privy to those proposals and knew what they were. I think the minister should let us know. I think it would be fair if the minister tabled for us in this house the proposals of the Canadian National Railways with regard to this debt structure. This analysis of the kind of depreciation the C.N.R. is involved in has shown that a debt structure has been developed from which C.N.R. can never get clear in terms of any kind of black gain on their profit sheet.

Supply-Transport
Another point I should like to make at this time is the question of the Matane-Ste. Anne des Monts railway. I have put some questions to the minister about this and I think he will agree that his replies have been less than informative. I can tell hon. members that this was a line which the C.N.R. did not want to build as part of its own structure, so it was launched, as an idea anyway, through a statute passed in this house which set up a government-owned railway which the C.N.R. would build and operate, but whose operating statements, revenues and so on, would be kept to one side as a special sort of government-owned operation. When that bill was before the house I raised some questions as to the economic viability of this road, but the bill went through despite this. I understand from the information which the minister has been kind enough to give me that the estimated costs are higher than those projected, and I should like to know how much higher they are. I feel we are entitled to know this, and I am sure that the people in Gaspe are entitled to know what are the government's intentions with regard to that road. I think the minister should also tell us whether the executive of the C.N.R. feel any more warmly toward this railway project than they did a year or two years ago. It seems to me that the government should be able to give a fairly quick and succinct answer in this regard.
There is one last point in relation to the C.N.R. that I wish to touch on. Mr. Gordon was quoted last January 25 in Labour, the weekly newspaper which is devoted to railway matters on behalf of the unions. The heading is: "Need a fighting morale, says Gordon of C.N.R.", and it goes on:
A strong plea for maintenance of and improvement of employee morale was made by president Donald Gordon of the Canadian National Railways at a meeting of the general chairmen's association of the railway unions held here. He said that "without good morale we couldn't run the railroad" and he asked the general chairmen, who represent union employees all across Canada, to help build this morale amongst their members.
I want to ask the minister whether he would do something that no previous transport minister has done. It is an extra imposition and burden, but I have raised this question of morale, as have other members, with Mr. Gordon before. Mr. Gordon has, to say the least, ridiculed our suggestions. He has said that things were never better, and suggested that if morale on the Canadian National Railway is bad it is probably the politicans who are responsible for it by leading these people along the wrong or improper path. I want to ask the minister whether as Minister of Transport he will consider taking on the responsibility of getting round and talking

to employees of the C.N.R. Everybody says that this question of their morale is important. Mr. Gordon says that he needs a fighting morale. The fighting morale I have seen is the desire on the part of a lot of C.N.R. employees to fight with Mr. Gordon.
I suggest that the minister could not make a better contribution to the Canadian National Railways than to take an interest in its employees. There has been, quite frankly, a tendency for previous ministers of transport to regard it as a hot potato and not to touch it; but I should like to see this minister go out and meet the men-not to call in the union heads, but go out and visit some of the terminal points and get to know the employees, and then arrive at his own conclusion as to why Mr. Gordon wants a fighting morale and claims that they have an excellent morale, when the rest of us who have a great many dealings with the people who work on the C.N.R. find evidence completely to contradict this. I think the minister, given the kind of level head and coolness which he has -I think we all recognize that he is not someone whose emotions will run wild with him- could do this job very well, and then we might reach the stage where a minister of transport could speak to this house about the Canadian National Railways and all the problems which we as members keep encountering with regard to it.
One of my colleagues, Mr. Chairman, is going to talk about the air situation so far as Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Airlines is concerned, but I should just like to put on the record two resolutions. If we had had the opportunity last year in our sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping to write a report on the operations of T.C.A. and the C.N.R., I had prepared two resolutions to bring before hon. members which I think speak for themselves. The first one was:
By action of the air transport board following a hearing in 1958, air line competition was introduced in Canada on the transcontinental route. The committee learned during its examination of T.C.A.'s 1961 annual report that that same air transport board has not exercised its authority to ensure that that competition be on a fair and equitable basis.
The reason why we were entitled, as I see it, to come to that conclusion was because on that particular route there are different fares in force as a result of the action of Canadian Pacific Airlines, and also there has been in a sense an extension of the rights which Canadian Pacific Airlines are exercising in light of what was originally expected in 1958.
The second resolution or point which I wanted to put into the report last year was this:

The air transport board, by its failure to disapprove either the T.C.A. domestic passenger tariff filed with it for effectiveness April 1, 1962, or the C.P.A. domestic passenger tariff in force prior to that date, has permitted to exist fare differentials with respect to both first class and economy fares on identical routes flown in the same type of aircraft by both the competing air lines. The committee understands that no similar fare discrepancies with respect to authorized fares exist in the industry, and it therefore strongly recommends that the air transport board be required to take corrective action at once.
The point about the milk runs that bothers some of us, and I have had representations from several air lines in western Canada, is that we do not know what the package is. We do not know what the deal is between the government, T.C.A. and Transair which has the contract at the present time. What did T.C.A. give in terms of dollar value in turning over the DC-3's and Viscounts to Transair? What undertaking did the minister give or the previous minister or the air transport board to Transair?
It is quite obvious to anyone who knows anything about air operations that Transair is losing money hand over fist at the present time. Yet the announcement was to the effect that it was taking this franchise without any subsidy. The only reason that those of us from the outside can figure that it would take over an obviously losing proposition would be that the equipment and services it got out of the deal from Trans-Canada Air Lines were enough to balance off for a period of time, and what some of us are apprehensive about is that once the value that Transair has received in this equipment has been balanced somewhat by the monthly losses that are building up we will get the cry again for a subsidy.
I want to make it clear that the New Democratic party is not arguing against a subsidy on the prairie route, but the point is that several other carriers with experience in that area insist that the route is impractical without some kind of subsidy, and apparently the settlement has been on the basis of no subsidy. I think we are entitled to know a bit more about this particular deal and I particularly should like to know if any great pressure was put on Trans-Canada Air Lines to get them to shift that equipment to Transair, for what I imagine was a very nominal fee.
One of the things that the minister of transport in the previous government took credit for, and I think to a degree deservedly so, was the great improvement in the shipbuilding industry as a result of the Conservative shipbuilding program. The former minister will remember that there are a few of us who have shipyards in our constituencies which have not benefited from the
Supply-Transport
shipbuilding program, and the subsidies. One of the complaints that we at the head of the lakes have, and it is a consistent complaint, is that our shipyard is owned by a very large corporation which also has yards at Collingwood, Kingston and Lauzon, Quebec. Naturally under the present set-up this firm has taken advantage of the subsidies and has directed the majority of its new construction into its yard at Lauzon and, secondarily, to its yard at Collingwood. That is accepted, I suppose, as the right of a private corporation; but the point I have made, and I know the hon. member for Fort William has made it also, is that any time the government is putting up that much of the cost for new shipping by way of subsidy, surely it must have the policy objective in mind of keeping our shipyards in this country to some kind of level both with regard to skills and plant. How effective is a shipbuilding policy if it leads to great concentrations and benefits in certain yards while other yards slip downhill both in terms of the quality of the workmen available and the kind of equipment they have?
I wish to say to the present minister that we think the shipbuilding subsidies have been an excellent thing, but we feel there should have been some provision in the act to permit some extra kind of incentive, not a penalty, to see that all yards in Canada have some opportunity for some of this construction. If the government should feel that even this kind of incentive to a private corporation such as Dominion Shipbuilding is something that philosophically they cannot accept, then I suggest that those yards that are not being given ships to construct by their corporate headquarters should be given first consideration when it comes to the construction of government ships. This is something again that we have been pushing for at the lakehead, but which has never been recognized.
Our shipyard at the lakehead in the main has diversified into a lot of lines and has done very well. It serves a very necessary repair yard. It is not the kind of shipyard that Canada can dispense with, because of its location and because of the great increase in shipping, particularly deep sea shipping through the St. Lawrence seaway and up to the head of the lakes. But what that shipyard needs to give it the kind of staff and the skills, and the opportunities to keep going, is an occasional new ship, government or private, and with the present structure of Dominion Shipbuilding this does not seem possible.
Another point about which I should like to ask the minister is whether he has given any

Supply-Transport
consideration to having a survey made of some of the harbours in Canada at present under harbour commissions constituted by this house, such as the lakehead harbour commission, and having them brought into a closer relationship with the national harbours board.

I should not like to suggest that at the lakehead, for example, we want the harbour commission to be taken over by the national harbours board at the present time, but I do feel that the national harbours board has experience and knowledge that would be of immense assistance to the lakehead harbour commission if it could be made available on some kind of co-operative or liaison basis. Finally, I would ask the minister when he is making his explanations to please tell us what role he played, and I should like a complete answer, in turning down or seeing that the government turned down the application for a radio station in Hull.
Where?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has just pointed out, the Department of Transport touches the lives of practically all Canadians and I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to bring before the minister a few of the most urgent needs of the people of my constituency. Before doing so I should like to associate myself with those who have expressed their compliments and good wishes to you personally, sir, and also to the Speaker and Deputy Speaker on assuming the high offices to which you have been called. I should also like to congratulate the minister on his appointment and to compliment him on the manner in which he has presented his first estimates to the house.
Before going further I should like to express my appreciation of the work that is being done by the very dedicated staff both here in Ottawa, and in my own province, and to voice my personal thanks for the

great co-operation and sympathetic consideration which I have always received from them whenever I have brought problems to their attention. I hope the minister will be able to come to my province before long. When he does he will discover that the office of his department in my province is seriously understaffed. The austerity program prevented new appointments being made, and I believe that the office has about half of the staff it requires to do its work efficiently. I know that the minister has not had time to inquire into all the facets of his department, but I would ask him to check on the salaries paid to top officials in his department, particularly in my own province, to ascertain how they compare with the salaries paid to the heads of other departments who have to carry comparable responsibility.
Now, practically all of my constituents live by the sea, and most of them live on the sea. It will be appreciated that aids to navigation have an important bearing on their lives in so far as they contribute to their personal safety and to their efforts to earn a livelihood. I want to express my thanks, on behalf of my constituents, for the many improvements that have been made in this regard during the past year. I hope that this improvement will be continued in the years ahead. I was glad to hear the minister say this morning that provision had been made for a marine haul-up at Clarenville. This is very fine, but Clarenville does not happen to be in my own riding. I want to impress upon the minister that the need in the riding of Burin-Burgeo is even more urgent than the need in Clarenville. The whole south coast, from Port aux Basques right around to St. John's, has no facilities at all for hauling out small boats for steamship inspection, maintenance and other purposes. There used to be one at Burin, but that has gone into disrepair and is no longer useable. Even the one at St. Pierre and Miquelon is now not as useful as it was. It is a very serious handicap to the people in the constituency when these facilities do not exist. We had hoped that they would have been provided long before this. We are waiting patiently in the hope that the provision of them will not be delayed very much longer.
I want to express my appreciation of the fact these estimates do contain some provision for expanding the ferry services between my province and the mainland. I want to urge the minister to speed up the construction of these ferries because I can assure him, from my own personal knowledge, that the travelling public is exposed to very serious inconvenience for the lack of these services. I do not want to expand on that, but I can say that I have seen people sitting

around without even a place to lie down because all the motel and hotel services at Port aux Basques or in the vicinity were completely filled. I should like the Minister of Transport to communicate with the management of Canadian National Railways, who should also have some responsibility to the travelling public to see that this situation is alleviated whenever possible by making sleeping cars available at the terminal when no other facilities are available.
I know the minister has not had time to examine all the different bits and pieces of administrative machinery in his department, but I want to bring to his attention one suggestion which I hope he will consider. My suggestion has to do with harbour administration. We do not have very many harbour boards, but I believe in decentralization of authority whenever possible. We do have in my province a number of pilotage commissions and a number of small harbour boards. They are set up under the act and their duties are separated. I believe it would tend to greater efficiency and better service if the scope of their authority could be extended. I see no reason why any efficient pilotage commission could not also have some responsibility for harbour administration. I see no reason why an effective harbour board could not also assume some of the duties of a pilotage commission. In small communities such as we have in my riding, the very same people act on these boards practically all the time. For all practical purposes, therefore, they are the same people wearing different hats.
I do know that a good deal of inconvenience could be eliminated if when we set up public harbours we did set up some local authority to which the harbourmaster could report, instead of having to report to the district office at St. John's. The district office, in turn, must get in touch with Ottawa before a decision can be reached. During the summertime, when we have short hours, with four o'clock closing on Friday and extra long week ends sometimes stretching over until Tuesday, long and unnecessary delays are experienced. If the minister would consider this suggestion, I think it would be beneficial to all concerned.
The last point I want to make is in connection with the subsidies for coastal shipping, to which the hon. member for Three Rivers referred this morning. I think that was a good move, but as the former minister himself pointed out it was designed mainly to help the shipyards. We do not have many shipyards in my province. We have one, possibly two. Most of our ships are built by the people who are going to sail 28902-5-137
Supply-Transport
them. These people go into the woods in the wintertime, cut timber for the frame and then proceed to build a ship. When these people try to take advantage of the subsidy, despite all the efforts of the maritime commission to help them with their problem, it is a very long and difficult operation before they can be assured they will receive the benefit of the subsidy. I think it should be possible to amend these regulations so as to take care of the cases which I have just described. I agree with the former minister of transport that we should be thinking in terms of expanding our merchant navy.
Our coastal fleet in Newfoundland has practically disappeared and there is not much incentive to replace it. Even with the subsidies granted, it is cheaper for the ship operators to have new ships built in Holland or Japan.
We are a nation of seafaring people, and we need small coastal ships to distribute our goods from the larger centres to the smaller communities. This type of service can best be supplied by small, locally built ships, which very often are built by the persons who are going to own and use them. I hope the minister will try and make it easier for such people to take advantage of the assistance that is available from his department.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about railway abandonment. I believe there should be a good long look taken before railway companies can go out and indiscriminately roll up tracks and abandon branch lines. When the former administration was in power there was a verbal agreement that all abandonment of branch lines would be frozen until there was a meeting called with the railways, the government, the large grain handling agencies in western Canada, and that in conjunction with the Mac-Pherson report an over-all policy would be worked out.
We in western Canada are very much concerned about this, as there is only one way of getting our grain out to the northern port of Churchill, the west coast, or to the head of the lakes, and that is by the railways. We have many grain handling devices on our farms, such as augers and blowers, but I repeat there is only one way of getting grain to the delivery points, and this is over the railways.
Railway abandonment will have a serious effect on Rosetown-Biggar constituency, which is one of the larger grain growing districts in Saskatchewan. I do not like to take individual cases, but there is one line for which there has been an application to abandon, and where this would affect many more people than the farmers. It is a short line running from Stewart Valley, a little village, out to the main C.P.R. line. At present the farmers

Supply-Transport
in the district haul their grain to the town of Stewart Valley, but if the railroad is abandoned and they haul their grain north they will have to cross the Saskatchewan river. To go east they would have to cross Stewart Valley, and if they have to haul it to the main line this would involve a distance of 40 or 50 miles in many cases.
The farmers and businessmen are not looking for passenger service or express service. Their whole plea is service for the handling of their grain. Stewart Valley is a thriving little town in the centre of a good wheat growing area. Businessmen in the district have their life savings tied up in small businesses, grocery stores, implement businesses and the like. If this line were abandoned there would be nothing else for them to do but move out, and leave their lifetime savings behind them and start all over again at some other point. This would cause considerable hardship to everyone in the district-and this is just one instance which will be repeated over and over again throughout the whole prairie region.
There is another matter which should be looked into in order to get a clear picture of the whole railway system in western Canada. I would like to bring to the attention of the committee the new policy which the C.N.R. intends to inaugurate in the very near future. It is known as the run-through, and is the doubling up on divisions.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has explained this very well, but I would like to call attention to just a few of the hardships it would cause at home divisional points, where the railwaymen make their homes. This is a case where train crews would run over two divisions, and it would cause a lot of unemployment.
One of the main towns in my constituency is the town of Biggar, which is known as a home division. If this run-through system is inaugurated it will take 150 men out of that little town of 3,000 people, 79 of whom are home owners. In many cases the railway employees who have built homes would have to pick up and leave, and go to wherever they were transferred, and when you take 79 home owners out of a little town of 3,000 people there is not much left for the town.
Biggar is not the best wheat growing area in my constituency, but it has a very good cattle industry. This alone would not support a town of its size, and if the railway employees had to move, as many of them who have built homes and are paying for them would have to do, there would be no chance of selling these homes, since there is no industry to bring people into the district.
I have talked with many railwaymen and all they are asking is a chance to work their

regular hours. They tell me that after eight hours in the cabs of fast moving freights, the strain is too great, and more accidents are caused after working that length of time in the cab. I know railway companies have as their motto, "safety first", and this is one of the things that should be taken into consideration. This is a matter at which we should take a good long look before the railways are allowed to go out and indiscriminately roll up the lines. I have a lot more to say on this point but there are other speakers who wish to participate in the debate. Therefore I ask the minister to give consideration to these things before the railway lines are abandoned.

Mr. Chairman, I am wondering whether I should answer some of the questions now, before too many accumulate. I shall try to confine my remarks to answering specific questions asked by hon. members. No doubt I will overlook a few, but this will be solely due to my system of doing my own reporting to myself, which I can assure hon. members is grossly inadequate.
I would like to put one question to the minister. On the orders of the day I asked a question concerning the Soulanges canal.

Perhaps I should answer that first, although I had hoped the hon. member would leave it until we came to the appropriate item when I would have the precise information in front of me. The situation is quite clear and it originated under the former minister.
As I understand the matter, there was an intimation from representatives of the government of the province of Quebec that they would take over the canal. Then the negotiations as to the detail of doing that were continued during the last year or two years- some considerable time anyway-and the result now is that we have an intimation that they are not interested in taking over the canal. Therefore it is a matter of determining the method of disposing of the canal.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to cut in on the minister but I would like to take this opportunity to point out that as far as the federal government was concerned, we had reached a conclusion on this matter of the Soulanges canal-

As a matter of fact, it is about a Department of Transport employee who had an accident and remained without help for three days. He was in a remote spot deprived of any means of communication, and it is only after three days that he managed to reach

a hospital. He had to pay all the costs. This employee lost the use of an eye, which, in my opinion, is a most serious injury. Now, because of this accident, this man is unable to hold a job today. He himself had to pay all medical and hospital costs. Unable to find work since the accident, he has to live on public welfare. Everybody knows that no company wants to hire a one-eyed worker.
I wish to point out this case to the house, because the Department of Transport claims it has no responsibility at all in the matter. This man had been hired by an employee of the Department of Transport who is a lighthouse keeper. According to the regulations of the Department of Transport, one of their employees is authorized to hire an assistant. However, that assistant is not paid by the lighthouse keeper, but directly by the department which sends him a cheque issued by the department. He is subject to income tax and his unemployment insurance dues are deducted at the source. In fact, he is a federal government employee who works with government appliances in a government building and on government property.
In fact, I know that as a Canadian and an ordinary citizen, if I hire someone to work on my property, I am responsible for him. For my own protection, I carry insurance against possible damage or injury to my employees. I know that the government must also have some, but I do not think it is justified in hiding itself behind a mere formality, thus refusing to assume its true responsibility in this matter.
The government must try to fill in this gap for, though it may be a small detail, it could now do much harm to Canadians employed by the government.
I therefore ask the minister-I do not blame him, for the fault lies in the regulations-but I ask the minister to make sure that these regulations are changed so that all lighthouse keepers may be protected by the Workmen's Compensation Act.
I hope that I have made that clear to the parliamentary secretary to the hon. minister and that he will take note of this remark.
In the Saguenay area, there is a magnificent lake, called lake St. John; no doubt everybody has heard about it. It is a wonderful resort area and no other can compare with it. It is also a place where there is plenty of fish and we have there a unique kind of fish called wananish.

You may ask what this has got to do with the Department of Transport? Well, Mr. Chairman, I am coming back immediately to the subject. Villages scattered all around the lake, overlooking it, with splendid beaches, and wharves erected by the Department of Public Works but under the responsibility of the Department of Transport. However, rocks and reefs are scattered around the lake and they are dangerous. Mr. Chairman, thousands of boats daily ply the waters of lake St. John. I would very much like to see the Department of Transport place signal buoys at the dangerous spots and if possible get rid of the larger reefs.
Mr. Chairman, in closing, I wish to thank the house for giving me the opportunity to express my views on some problems of the Department of Transport.

Mr. Chairman, like many other hon. members who have spoken I should like to congratulate the minister upon assuming his new responsibilities as Minister of Transport. I have known him personally since I came to the house and other members of my family have met him. We have always found him to be a very congenial gentleman and certainly very easy to get along with.
I wish to deal with one phase of the activities of this department which affects western Canada, which is dealt with in the report of the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. Before doing so I would like to reply to the minister's remarks regarding the discretion of the B.B.G. and ministerial discretion. I think he would agree with me, as he is also a lawyer, that, like the board of transport commissioners, they have certain judicial discretion which they exercise as an administrative body. That discretion is set out by statute. The B.B.G. also has discretionary powers set out by statute. Just as the cabinet can decide to veto or accept a recommendation or decision of the board of transport commissioners, so can the minister decide to accept or reject a judgment of that board. I fail to see very much difference in that particular kind of discretion.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Would the hon. member not agree that the two pieces of legislation are not parallel at all. I refer to the hon.
28902-5-138J
Supply-Transport
member's reference to the board of transport commissioners and the cabinet. The Radio Act and the other legislation dealing with the board of broadcast governors are quite different. One piece of legislation sets out a duty for the board of broadcast governors and a duty for the minister; and the board of broadcast governors fulfilled its duty and the minister fulfilled his duty.

Yes, but I was merely putting that forward as an analogy. I think the minister will go this far, that there is still a legal discretion which he can exercise, irrespective of whether that power is spelled out by that particular legislation. I have not been briefed on this matter recently but I say the minister has a discretion and he can exercise that discretion. That is a discretion within the realm of the responsibility of the minister himself. Then there is the discretion of the board, whose powers are set out in the act. However, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into a legal argument on the powers of the B.B.G. or the powers of the board of transport commissioners. I was merely pointing this out as an analogy and saying that he still has a discretion which he can exercise, and a discretion which he does exercise under the law, that is his responsibility.
I am rather sorry that the Minister of Agriculture is absent on Fridays, because on one occasion in the house he said-and this matter will be relevant to the question before the committee-he was praying that the rain was stopping in western Canada. I would point out that in western Canada at the moment there is growing one of the largest crops seen on the prairies and it appears from reports of the wheat pool and the grain elevator companies that there is going to be a bumper crop. No other industry in Canada, in my opinion, is affected more by transportation than is the agricultural industry, particularly in western Canada. I recall the terms of reference being laid down when the royal commission on transportation was set up, and the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, stating that the Crowsnest pass agreement was the economic Magna Carta of western Canada. I think that is true. This was an agreement entered into with the railways at that time, and that type of agreement which controls the freight rates on grain is the economic Magna Carta of western Canada. The margin which exists between profit and the costs of production of grain might easily be wiped out if the freight rates on western Canada grain were increased.

Supply-Transport
I also recall certain statements of hon. gentlemen then in opposition, particularly those of the present Minister of Justice, who said he thought the Crowsnest pass freight rates were like chains or shackles around the railway companies. It was set out very clearly by the then government, the Conservative government, and by the then prime minister that there would be no change in the Crowsnest pass freight rates.
I wish to come to grips with another question for a few moments, because the hon. member from Rosetown-Biggar discussed the question of rail line abandonment. I want not only to discuss the question of rail line abandonment as far as freight is concerned, but also as far as passengers are concerned. I should also like to point out why certain lines should not be abandoned. The Minister of Transport did answer some questions in this regard today. However, I think when we are dealing with the question of the abandonment of railway lines, whether passenger or freight, we must first of all have a national policy on the subject. I think we should look carefully at what was recommended by the MacPherson royal commission in this regard. In dealing with the abandonment of passenger railway lines I should like to take issue at this time with the abandonment of a particular line between the city of Calgary and the city of Saskatoon, known by people in that area as the Goose lake line. Those passenger trains were taken off, and at the present time, except for T.C.A., they find there is no other means of transportation between those two cities by anything like a direct route. There is a bus, but it stops at a little place called Oyen inside the border of Alberta. It spends seven hours there; passengers are forced to spend seven hours in the town before continuing their journey to Calgary. I recall the hon. member for Lethbridge asking the Prime Minister a question about this, and the right hon. gentleman said he would look into it personally. But the line has been abandoned and nothing has been done about it to date.
I think we should look at what the MacPherson commission had to say in this regard. It was certainly not in favour of abandoning lines holus-bolus. I realize the minister has suggested that this is not the occasion to get into a detailed discussion about the abandonment of railways, but this is a subject of such importance to agriculture that I hope I may be allowed to make a few observations on it and to remind hon. members of what was said by the royal commission on transportation set up by the previous government under Mr. MacPherson. People familiar with
IMr. Woolliams.]
transportation in all its phases gave evidence before this commission, and it is on the basis of this evidence that the recommendations were made. On the subject of the passenger service I should like to refer to volume 1 of that report, dated March, 1961, page 60, where it states:
To facilitate the reduction of the passenger deficits, we recommend that the pertinent statutes be amended to enable the railways, upon application to the board of transport commissioners, to remove any uneconomic passenger service except when the board is satisfied that no reasonable alternative public highway exists.
I think that had been overlooked when they decided to remove the passenger train service between Saskatoon, a city of 100,000 people and Calgary, a city of 300,000, without any alternative method of transportation being available as far as the railway is concerned.
If we read volumes 2 and 3 of the report we find there is evidence to suggest that the provision of a passenger service in Canada is uneconomic, no matter to how great an extent the facilities are used. As an example, I understand that at one time there were two luxury passenger trains known as the Canadian and the Dominion. I am told by the employees of the Dominion train that even when it was packed to capacity they were losing money on the route from Calgary to the east. So it is obviously not good enough to be able to say only that the service itself is uneconomic. These trains should only be removed-I make the suggestion to the minister-when, in addition to being uneconomic, the cabinet is satisfied that no reasonably satisfactory alternative public highway exists. There is a public highway between the two cities I have named but it is not paved all the way and, surely, if a passenger train is to be removed, these things should be taken into consideration. As I have said, at the present time, passengers on the 400 mile route by bus have to spend seven hours waiting in a small town, in some cases without proper accommodation.
Certain recommendations were made by the commission with regard to freight. I think it must be acknowledged by any government that a revolution is taking place in western Canada. I think that in the next ten years we are going to see a new picture. It has to come, it is true, in these days of automation which are having such an undeniable impact on the farmers of western Canada. It is now possible to take away 500 or 800 bushels of grain in a truck. It is, therefore, easier to take that grain a greater distance than was formerly the case, and it is possible to conceive,

especially as these railways are being subsidized by the taxpayers' money, that some of these lines may have to be abandoned. But they must be abandoned in some kind of order. In the near future much larger elevators will probably be built to replace small country elevators every eight, ten or twelve miles. In the meantime, a definite plan must be set up so that the abandonment of lines where necessary will not cause hardship to our farmers.
I can recall a debate in which the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was discussing the building of a large elevator in the town of Tisdale, the gateway to the Carrot river valley, and many thousands of acres of magnificent farmland. The minister told the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale that he did not think this was a proper place for an elevator. But maybe the hon. member in question has put his finger on the revolution which is taking place in the west, because I can see the day when these larger elevators will be built in western Canada in much larger numbers as grain is taken to market over longer distances.
Be this as it may, lines cannot be taken up without a definite plan in mind. This is why the former government appointed a royal commission to make certain that a national plan will be set up so as to avoid hardship. I suggest to the minister that he and his department should study most carefully the recommendation made by Mr. MacPherson and his commission in this regard. I can say this of Mr. M. A. MacPherson, a lawyer from Regina: he is a man who has had much experience not only of agriculture but of railroading in western Canada, and of the economy of western Canada in general. At page 65 of the report, the following paragraph appears:
In the light of these considerations, of the analysis presented in chapter 2, and of the recommendations for meeting passenger service deficits and the problem of light density lines, we recommend that in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway a sum of $9 million annually shall be paid on behalf of the export grain traffic as a contribution to constant costs. This should place export grain traffic in a position comparable to other segments of traffic in the light of the permissive level of earnings.
That was the answer to the complaint made by the railways. In spite of this treatment by the royal commission the railways were saying at that time they were losing money on the freighting of grain from western Canada and the lakehead to Vancouver and Port Churchill. Then they say:
Making adjustments necessary due to the different financial structure of the Canadian National Railways, the payment recommended to that company as a contribution on behalf of the export grain traffic to overheads is $7.3 million.
Supply-Transport
The shipping of grain is one commodity which the railways ship differently from any other. In western Canada you see these grain trains going through which, particularly under diesel power, are almost a mile in length, consisting of cars carrying grain across to the ports, where it is loaded on to boats and thus reaches the export market. The commission said that if losses are occasioned in the shipping of grain-the C.N.R. shows a deficit in practically all its operations although the C.P.R. does show a profit *-the government should set up a subsidy so that the returns on that commodity will be comparable with others.
Then on page 66 of the report they say:
When the process of rationalizing plant by the elimination of rail lines occasioning a system net loss has substantially progressed, or when it appears that there has been any other substantial change in the overhead costs of the railways, the constant costs of the railways should be re-evaluated. After these re-evaluations the remuneration paid on behalf of the movement of grain and grain products to export positions at statutory and related rates should be adapted to the changed situation.
The commission say that there should not be any change in the Crowsnest pass freight rates. When the Minister of Justice, who is not here today, was in opposition he said that these freight rates were shackles around the railways. But the commission say that if there is any loss, subsidies must be applied to make these commodities comparable with others. The former prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, said that the Crowsnest pass rates were the economic Magna Carta of western Canada and should not be interfered with, because the margin between a loss and a profit is so narrow on wheat farms, with the high cost of machinery, that these people could not stay in business. That is the point I wish to make particularly, when dealing with estimates, and in reference to the recommendations made by the royal commission on transportation. I sincerely hope that this commission will not suffer the fate of other royal commissions appointed under another government, and lie on the shelf in the library, because some fine recommendations are made here by a body of men who heard the evidence of people who understood business and industry. The royal commission on transportation was long overdue. Their report is now in the hands of departmental officials and it should be checked thoroughly before the government commence abandoning rail lines holus-bolus.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned another problem in western Canada concerning the loss of markets. One of our problems is getting wheat to the ports. One of the problems the former government were faced with in western Canada when

Supply-Transport
they took office in 1957 was that box cars were unavailable. There were many sidings, villages and towns which for months on end had no trains taking out wheat. Most of the quotas in 1956 and 1957 were either two or five bushels per acre, and many farmers could not get grain to the elevator because there were no box cars. The time to think about these things is not in September or October when the problem arises; I suggest with respect to the minister that the time to be thinking about this problem is now. If you recall, Mr. Chairman, there was a report made by Mr. Bracken, and as a result the allocation of box cars certainly improved. Anyone in western Canada will admit that the transportation of grain and other commodities out of western Canada improved under the Conservative government 100 per cent compared with the situation under the previous government with C. D. Howe.
When dealing with the question of line abandonment I might say that I do not think the board of transport commissioners have the capacity to deal with all the applications. I say this with no disrespect to the personnel of the board. I have appeared before them and they are fine gentlemen. But if they are to consider each application individually they will not be able to do so in an orderly fashion. The board must either be enlarged or some other body set up in order to consider a properly planned abandonment, so as to protect the agricultural industry which for the last five or six years has been in a pretty healthy state. There has to be a gradual working out of rail abandonment which will logically fit into the resolution which has taken place. New economic circumstances must be considered if railways are abandoned holus-bolus. Not only must you consider the industry, but the people and farmers who live in the towns, villages and cities, and also the personnel of the railways themselves. That is one recommendation which I would make.
In spite of the fact that the minister says he has legislation hot in the oven, I would like to hear what is the policy of the present Liberal government with regard to rail abandonment in western Canada. I hope he does not reply in the way he replied to the hon. member for Port Arthur and say that he will discuss it on another day or two weeks from now. This government assured the Canadian people that they were people of decision. Well, we have had the first 60 days, and we know that it will take another 60 days to undo what they did in that first 60 days. We want to know what the government is going to about rail abandonment, how it will occur, what board will have the power
[Mr. Woolliams.l
to make decisions, and whether the government recognize that a revolution is taking place as far as agriculture and the marketing of grain is concerned. What is the government going to do this fall when western Canada produces 600 million bushels of grain? A recent article was put out by the C.N.R. to the effect that there is a shortage of box cars. Is the government meeting with officials and discussing the problem with the companies? Now is the time to build new box cars to haul the grain from the particular marketing areas in western Canada to the ports. We have heard a lot about unemployment, and this would certainly help this problem as well. I should like to hear from the minister what is his reaction to the recommendations made by the MacPherson commission on transportation.

Supply-Transport
Lake St. John, have made a plea that Trans-Canada Air Lines should purchase their new jet aircraft from Canadair, and should purchase the Caravelle aircraft. It may well be that Trans-Canada will ultimately select this particular aircraft, but I believe that the corporation should be left free to make its own decision. Their hands are tied to a certain extent. From what we have heard today I believe they are committed to choosing an aircraft with a large amount of Canadian content, but there are two or three companies in competition to supply the aircraft. I should like to see this decision based upon economics and not upon what I would call political economy.
It has been proven in the past that this has been a good policy. Not too many years ago attempts were made to pressure Trans-Canada into buying the CL-44 aircraft and I think events have proven that their decision to obtain the DC-8 was the correct one, because for their particular use the DC-8 has been more versatile. I say again that I deplore the efforts made by politicians in this house to force the corporation to take a particular plane. I hope Trans-Canada is left free to make this decision themselves. They may come to the decision some members want but it should be an independent decision.
There is another matter related to air services to which I should like to make some reference at this time. I refer to a particular group of employees of the Department of Transport, employees who play a most important role in the operation of aircraft in Canada. These are the people who man the air control towers. I imagine that from time to time most members of this house who travel in aircraft are aware of the responsibilities of the pilot and crew. I am not at all sure that they are aware of the tremendous responsibilities which rest on the people who direct air traffic. This responsibility is growing year by year. As aircraft become bigger and faster, the importance of keeping them in the right place at the right altitude, and correctly spaced apart, becomes increasingly difficult.
I believe that this group of employees have made representations to the government concerning their pay and working conditions. If I may put it briefly, their pay is about 33 per cent lower than that of persons in the United States doing the same kind of work. I have watched them at work, and it is very nerve-wracking work. You sit for hours in front of a screen, guiding aircraft. In fact, close to the airport the air traffic controller is the actual navigator of the aircraft. I hope the department will give careful consideration to the representations

of the air traffic controllers because they have a most responsible job and I believe they should be well rewarded for it.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude on the point on which I started, namely, the necessity for a department of civil aviation in this country. I should like to read some appropriate sections from a recent editorial in the Montreal Gazette of June 8. I quote:
The air transport association of Canada has submitted a set of recommendations to the Prime Minister which it believes would bring greater cohesion and harmony to the entire air transport field ...
To establish a department of civil aviation would be to alter the trend set by the formation of the Department of Transport in 1936, for the transport department combined marine, railway and civil aviation services.
Yet there is much to be said for this recommendation. The responsibilities of the Minister of Transport are extremely heavy. The growth of the past 20 years has been sufficiently great to make it doubtful if any one person can really master all the duties for which the minister is directly or indirectly responsible.
For in addition to administering the department, the minister must report to parliament for Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines, the national harbours board and other bodies. The field of civil aviation has undergone such an expansion that a separate department might well be justified, and the proposal deserves careful consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a few remarks to the Minister of Transport in connection with the Waterloo-Wellington airport economic survey which has been mentioned to his deputy minister by the hon. members for Wellington South and Waterloo South. This airport has become so popular that extra accommodation is necessary in order to provide adequate service.
About three years ago, approval was extended by this department to the former government for lights which have been installed. This addition to the airport has encouraged the Waterloo-Wellington airport commission each year to go on to greater things. With this in mind, the airport commission has had a survey made which I understand has been sent to the deputy minister for his study. I sincerely hope that this department will give the economic survey serious consideration and will be instrumental in having steps taken to have some of the initial stages of the recommendations commenced as soon as possible.
As the minister is no doubt aware, the need for greater facilities at this fine airport is becoming urgent. A very comprehensive report has been prepared by Mr. W. O. Chisholm, a consulting engineer, as a guide for future development of the airport. The report was compiled with the co-operation of the officers of the Department of Transport in Toronto, and Mr. D. P. Glenn, director of civil aviation at Toronto has intimated that the

project will be progressed through Mr. J. R. Baldwin, deputy minister of transport, with the recommendation that an economic survey be made in order to secure authority to implement the first two stages of the plan as soon as possible.
For the information of the minister, I should like to advise him that the Water loo-Wellington airport is located on a 658 acre site in Waterloo township near Breslau, Ontario. Serving primarily the counties of Waterloo and Wellington, the airport was constructed in 1948 with the aid of the federal Department of Transport and is operated by the Waterloo-Wellington airport commission. Represented on the commission in 1963 are the municipalities of Kitchener, Guelph, Galt, Waterloo, Preston, and Waterloo township. The members of this commission are outstanding citizens of our area and have given much of their time and money to bring about the excellent progress that has been made.
The airport consists of two surface runways and a grassed strip, in a triangular layout. The prevailing winds favour the two surfaced runways for the major part of the time. Published information regarding the airport is as follows: airport elevation, 1,030 feet; runway 13-31, 4,100 feet; runway 7-25, 3,700 feet; grass strip, 2,800 feet; runway 13-31 is lighted for night flying. Aircraft fuel and maintenance services are available as well as hangar storage facilities.
The airport is the headquarters for the Water loo-Wellington flying club, and Swift Airways Limited has established a commercial aircraft centre at the site. In all, the airport is being operated very progressively and is situated in the centre of a prosperous business and industrial complex. The design and development of the original airport was well planned and the site is well suited. With few exceptions the surrounding land use is presently agricultural, so that any necessary additional restrictions in the area may be imposed at this time with a minimum of difficulty. There is a keen interest in flying in this area, as well as an increasing business use and realization of the importance of the airport facilities. Yes, this airport is very important, as we have well over 600 industries in Waterloo North, Waterloo South and Wellington South counties, along with many others within a radius of 25 miles.
Considering the relatively short time the airport has been in existence, the activity which has developed is remarkable. This activity has reached the point where taxiway facilities and a plan for future development are required. It is my sincere hope that in the near future members of the Waterloo-Wellington airport commission may have the
Supply-Transport
opportunity of meeting with the minister and his deputy so that this economic survey may be fully discussed. Then, perhaps, in the near future this airport may become one of Canada's most important in the handling of commercial and passenger plane service.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three matters I should like to discuss briefly while we are on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport. There are some other matters I might prefer to bring up when we get to the details of the estimates. Like other members, I am pleased that the new Minister of Transport is having an early opportunity of bringing in the estimates of his department for the consideration of the committee. I think all hon. members have appreciated the constructive, co-operative attitude which the minister displayed in answering various questions put to him so far.
I wish to deal briefly with the alteration announced for harbour commissions. Earlier the minister referred to the fact that certain legislation was being introduced in the other place. I have no idea what approach that legislation is going to take, but I think it indicated there would be some move to coordinate more closely the operations of the national harbours board and the various independent harbour commissions across the country. I hope this may have some relation to the information brought to my attention, that the two appointees of the government to the Port Alberni board of harbour commissioners have received notice that their term of office will not be renewed.
Up to a point I would not deny that there may have been certain political overtones in the appointment of the commissioners whose terms are expiring, but other commissioners connected with that board hope that appointees will not be decided from a political point of view. Going back to the genesis of the Port Alberni board of harbour commissioners, there were certain political aspects to that situation which involved certain internal relations within the minister's party. Although I have never been associated with his party, I may have become better acquainted with those details than the minister himself. However that is ancient history, and the only reason I bring it to his attention is that I hope when he may be considering the renewal of terms of office of government members he will not be governed entirely by political considerations.
Another relatively minor matter I wish to raise has to do with the radio regulations and the situation that governs the installation of radio broadcasting and receiving equipment, particularly in the marine field on the Pacific coast. I have made some inquiries as to the

Supply-Transport
availability of a consolidation of the regulations issued, and according to the best of my information the current regulations are not available in consolidated form. I suggest they should be made available in that form to all hon. members, to those who sell the equipment and to those who instal it. I also hope such a consolidation could be easily kept up to date, without those concerned having to consult the various issues of the Canada Gazette, part II, where various amending regulations appear from time to time.
While the old saying that ignorance of the law is no excuse, may be a fine principle in theory, I believe hon. members would agree that as regulations become more and more complex, particularly in the technical fields, provision should be made by this house whereby the public can have easy access to a knowledge of the law, particularly where it exists in regulatory form under the authority granted by parliament to the governor in council.
Another matter I wish to raise involves a question of principle. A situation has developed which requires a re-assessment of the terms of reference which have been given to the air transport board in the performance of the duties assigned to it under the Aeronautics Act. I am referring to a situation in which one of the air lines on the west coast, Pacific Western Airlines, was involved in a strike with certain of its employees. The air transport board, in accordance with the principles under which it operates, had given authority to Pacific Western Airlines to operate what constituted a monopoly in transportation service on their class 1 route between Vancouver and Port Hardy. However, when the strike developed, in accordance with the established principles of labour legislation the unions concerned established picket lines.
Many of the normal patrons of Pacific Western Airlines are members of unions and they object quite strongly to the idea of crossing a legally established picket line. This situation put the air transport board in a rather invidious position, because its members apparently understood their terms of reference to apply only within the narrow confines of the text of the Aeronautics Act. In effect, by their action they placed people in the position where they had the alternative of crossing a picket line or not being able to travel freely between their normal place of work and the place where many of them live. The loggers of the Pacific coast are organized into a union, the international woodworkers of America, and the union took steps to enable its members to avoid the dilemma in which they had been placed. They had no transportation at all, or they

had to travel by a very roundabout, circuitous, time consuming and expensive route.
In order to solve this dilemma the union tried to arrange to charter an aircraft from one of the other air lines, which would in effect have enabled the members of that organization to get back and forth without the necessity of using the facilities of Pacific Western Airlines while this strike was in progress. They made the charter arrangement, and one flight actually took place on April 2 this year. However, the air transport board took the initiative and ordered B.C. Air Lines, which was the firm from which the charter had been obtained, to cease and desist operating under any such charter, on the ground that it roughly paralleled the flight route of the established P.W.A. class 1 service and was in effect an attempt to circumvent the decision of the air transport board to grant that licence.
I would not suggest that in the ordinary terms of reference this particular arrangement was not, in effect, one which would have circumvented the protection which had been granted to Pacific Western Airlines in operating their class 1 service. But I would suggest that the minister and this house should make it clear that in circumstances such as these the air transport board should operate under somewhat broader terms of reference than they in fact operated under in this case. I think few hon. members of this house-at least, I hope few hon. members of this house-would question that there is the well established right for citizens in a free country to choose not to cross a picket line which has been established as a result of a labour dispute. I think that should be recognized as being a very basic, individual freedom in this country. To my mind it is a matter of great regret that a body set up and operating under the authority of parliament should have followed a course of action which in effect denied that right to certain Canadian citizens.
For this reason, Mr. Chairman, I certainly hope the minister will take a lead in seeing that the terms of reference of the air transport board are such that a similar situation will not again develop. As a matter of fact, as I understand the present provisions of the Aeronautics Act it is quite within the powers of the air transport board and the minister, or of the governor in council, to deal with a situation such as this as and when it arises. Section 13 of the Aeronautics Act says:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council, the board may make regulations:
Then it gives quite a list of them. Paragraph (f) says:
Excluding from the operation of the whole or any part of this part or any regulation, order or

I would suggest that within the authority of the air transport board and the governor in council there is, under the present provisions of the Aeronautics Act, authority for the air transport board, with the approval of the governor in council, to exercise the proper discretionary powers that are set out in section 13, which would have covered a situation of the kind I have been attempting to describe to the committee. The proper course of action in this instance would have been for the air transport board to raise this matter with the governor in council, with a recommendation that for the duration of this particular dispute the normal provisions of the protected class 1 licence under which Pacific Western Airlines was operating should not apply in a way which would, in effect, give Pacific Western Airlines a monopoly position when the union concerned, at its own expense and for the benefit entirely of its own membership, was prepared to make an arrangement which would enable those members so desiring to avoid crossing this picket line.
